- If sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.7) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.3) or volatile, model often underestimates downside risk; add buffer below forecast or anticipate sharper declines.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overcorrects and forecasts a prolonged upward trend — adjust downward by 5–10% of spike magnitude.
- Model shows strong mean reversion bias in early forecast periods (e.g., first 5–7 days of 30d forecast) — if true outcome diverges early, shift mean toward actual recent history.
- When sentiment history shows repeated high-low swings (e.g., 0.8 → 0.1 → 0.8), model tends to lag in capturing sentiment shifts — align forecast midpoint with sentiment peak/trough timing.
- If true outcome shows early “rebound” after a dip (e.g., 68 → 74 → 76), model often underreacts — increase forecast slope in first 3–5 days post-dip.
- For 30d forecasts, if first 5 days show consistent upward drift, model often overestimates later days — cap forecast growth after 5–7 days unless sentiment remains bullish.
